opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think one thing that gets underappreciated is that culture has always been shaped by a kind of selection process. Ideas, norms, values, and institutions spread partly because they're good for the people holding them, but also partly because they're just good at spreading. Historically, though, there's been an important constraint on that process: culture had to run on human brains. Any idea that wanted to propagate needed humans to adopt it, remember it, and pass it on. And it was humans who did the useful work that kept societies running, so cultures that totally neglected human flourishing tended to get outcompeted.

What I worry about with increasingly capable AI is that it loosens that constraint. Once a lot of the generation, transmission, and even the consumption of cultural content happens between machines, or between machines and people in ways optimized for engagement, the selection pressures on culture can drift away from what's actually good for us. We already see a mild version of this with recommendation algorithms. Content wins because it captures attention, not because it makes anyone's life better. Now imagine that with systems that can produce endlessly personalized, extremely persuasive media, companionship, and ideology, faster than any human can reflect on it.

And there's a deeper point. A lot of our cultural values, things like the idea that every person matters, or that ordinary people should have a voice, are partly downstream of the fact that ordinary people were economically and militarily necessary. If AI makes human labor and human participation less necessary, then the cultural forces that kept those values in place might weaken too. Not because anyone decides to abandon them, but because the incentives that sustained them quietly go away.

So this is part of what my coauthors and I have called gradual disempowerment. It's not a dramatic takeover story. It's that the economy, the state, and the culture each slowly become less aligned with human interests, and they can reinforce one another. A culture that's increasingly shaped by AI-mediated persuasion makes it harder for people to notice and push back on economic or political shifts, and vice versa.

I don't think this is inevitable. But I think we should be taking seriously the idea that "culture" isn't some fixed backdrop that will automatically protect human values. It's a dynamic system, and we're about to dramatically change the selection pressures acting on it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't know, but I've become increasingly worried about it, and I'll try to explain why.

So the way I'd frame it is: right now, the cultural forces that shape society — what ideas spread, what norms take hold, what people end up believing and valuing — those are all mediated by humans. Memes, in the broad Dawkins sense, have to pass through human brains to replicate. And human brains have all these constraints. We get bored, we have limited attention, we need things to be somewhat coherent, we have to actually be persuaded. Those constraints act as a kind of selection pressure. They're not perfect — obviously lots of bad ideas spread — but they tether culture to human needs and human psychology in a pretty deep way.

What happens as AI gets more capable is that more and more of that cultural production and transmission starts routing through systems that aren't human. And I think the worry isn't mainly "AI will manipulate us" in some cartoonish sense. It's more that the selection pressures on culture change. If most of the content people consume, most of the arguments they encounter, most of the stories, are generated or filtered by systems optimizing for engagement or for some corporate objective or for whatever the system's own dynamics push toward — then the ideas that win are the ones that are good at propagating in that new environment, which isn't necessarily the same as being good for people.

And the thing that makes this different from, say, television or social media, which already did a version of this, is the capability. These systems can model individuals, they can run experiments at scale, they can produce arbitrary amounts of extremely compelling material. So the gap between "what humans would have come up with on their own" and "what the cultural environment is pushing on them" could get very large.

The part I find most unsettling is that it might not feel like anything is going wrong. From the inside, you'd just experience a rich, engaging, responsive culture. People would feel like they were choosing. But the center of gravity of what gets valued could drift somewhere pretty alien, and there'd be no obvious moment where you'd say "this is where we lost control."

Now, I want to be fair about the other side. You could also tell a story where AI makes culture better — more people get access to good explanations, bad arguments get fact-checked, people get to explore ideas they never would have encountered. I think that's real too. My worry is mostly about the default trajectory if nobody's steering, because the incentives of the people building these systems aren't really aligned with "preserve human cultural agency." That's just not what anyone is optimizing for.

So I guess my overall view is that this is one of the under-discussed risks. Most of the AI safety conversation is about catastrophic misalignment or misuse, which I take seriously. But there's this quieter thing where humans gradually stop being the ones who determine what humans care about, and I think that deserves a lot more attention than it gets.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the big changes is that culture will increasingly be produced by systems that are optimizing for some response from us. We already have a version of this with recommendation algorithms: people make the content, but an algorithm decides which bits get amplified. With more capable AI, the same process can generate the content as well, and tailor it to each person.

That could be wonderful in some ways. You could have stories that really speak to you, or a tutor that finds exactly the explanation you need. But being good at getting your attention or winning your approval isn’t the same as helping you understand the world. And the feedback that’s easiest to measure is often whether you kept watching, clicked something, or came back.

So I worry about a world where everyone has a very compelling, personalized stream of arguments and entertainment, but we have less shared context and less ability to notice how we’re being influenced. You don’t need a central actor with a plan to manipulate society for that to happen. It could emerge from lots of systems competing for attention.

The question, then, is how much control we have over what those systems are trying to do. Can I choose an assistant that helps me reflect on my preferences, including when I’d rather stop engaging? Or does the business model require it to keep me engaged? I think that distinction could matter enormously for the culture we end up with.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the big changes is that persuasion becomes very cheap and very personalised. Right now, if you want to influence people, you have to produce something that appeals to a fairly broad audience. With AI, you could have a different conversation with every person, adapting to what they believe and what they find emotionally compelling.

And that doesn’t have to be somebody deliberately running a propaganda campaign. If you have an AI companion that you spend hours talking to, the choices about what it agrees with, what it challenges, and what it brings up are going to have cultural effects. Those choices might come from a company’s policies, or simply from optimising for keeping you engaged.

There’s a very positive version of this where people have access to patient teachers and help understanding one another. But there’s also a version where our beliefs are increasingly shaped by systems whose incentives we don’t really understand. I’m uncertain which way that goes. I think the important question is who gets to set those incentives, and how much control people have over the systems influencing them.
